If you have measured several variables in your **cross-sectional** study, you can display an (⚠️ apparent) relationship between them using various methods.

## Exercise 4

Calculate the **risk difference**, **relative risk**, and **odds ratio** for the association between diabetes and periodontitis.

```{=html}
<div class="spss-workflow">
  <div class="spss-workflow-header">
    <span class="spss-workflow-badge">SPSS</span>
    <span class="spss-workflow-title">Workflow Guide</span>
  </div>
  <ol class="spss-steps">
    <li>
      <div class="step-content">
        <div class="instruction-flow">
          <span class="step">Analyze</span>
          <span class="arrow">→</span>
          <span class="step">Descriptive Statistics</span>
          <span class="arrow">→</span>
          <span class="step">Crosstabs</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </li>
    <li>
      <div class="step-content">
        In the Crosstabs dialog, click <span class="spss-button">Cells...</span>, under <strong>Percentages</strong> select <strong>Row</strong>, then click <strong>Continue</strong>.
      </div>
    </li>
    <li>
      <div class="step-content">
        Click <span class="spss-button">Statistics...</span>, check <strong>Risk</strong>, and click <strong>Continue</strong>.
      </div>
    </li>
  </ol>
</div>
```

**Calculate manually:**

::: {.formula-grid}
::: {.formula-card}
**Risk difference (RD)**

Subtract the percentage values:
$$
RD = p_{\text{diabetic w/ perio}} - p_{\text{non-diabetic w/ perio}}
$$
:::

::: {.formula-card}
**Relative risk (RR)**

Divide the percentage values:
$$
RR = \frac{p_{\text{diabetic w/ perio}}}{p_{\text{non-diabetic w/ perio}}}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.formula-card .formula-card-wide}
**Odds ratio (OR)**

The odds ratio compares the odds of periodontitis between people with diabetes and people without diabetes.

::: {.odds-grid}
::: {.odds-step}
**Diabetic group**

$$
\text{Odds}_{\text{diabetic}} = \frac{a}{b}
$$
:::

::: {.odds-step}
**Non-diabetic group**

$$
\text{Odds}_{\text{non-diabetic}} = \frac{c}{d}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.odds-final}
**Final odds ratio**

$$
OR = \frac{a/b}{c/d} = \frac{a \times d}{b \times c}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.notation-card}
**Notation**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:------:|:--------|
| $a$ | Diabetics **with** periodontitis |
| $b$ | Diabetics **without** periodontitis |
| $c$ | Non-diabetics **with** periodontitis |
| $d$ | Non-diabetics **without** periodontitis |
:::

<details open>

Let the 2×2 table be:

|              | Periodontitis (+) | Periodontitis (−) |
|--------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Diabetic     | ( a )             | ( b )             |
| Non-diabetic | ( c )             | ( d )             |

</details>

::: {.poll-calc #p2-t4}
Enter your results (two decimals).

- [Risk difference (RD)]{.calc answer="12" tol="0.3" unit="%" mistakes="-12: Negative sign – subtract the non-diabetics from the diabetics. | 1.88: That is a ratio (RR) – the RD is a difference."}
- [Relative risk (RR)]{.calc answer="1.88" tol="0.02" mistakes="0.53: Groups swapped – divide diabetics by non-diabetics. | 0.34: Divided within the diabetic row – that is the odds a/b. | 0.86: Used the “no periodontitis” column."}
- [Odds ratio (OR)]{.calc answer="2.19" tol="0.02" mistakes="0.46: Inverted – OR = (a·d) / (b·c). | 1.88: That is the relative risk, not the odds ratio. | 0.34: Only the odds of the diabetics (a/b)."}
:::

::: {.poll #p2-t4-or correct="3"}
Which statement correctly describes the odds ratio you calculated?

- It is the difference in the risk of periodontitis between the two groups, in percentage points.
- It shows that diabetes causes periodontitis.
- It compares the odds of periodontitis in people with diabetes with the odds in people without diabetes.
- It tells you how many times higher the risk of periodontitis is in people with diabetes.

::: poll-explanation
The OR compares **odds**, not risks. The risk ratio here is the RR = 1.88. The two differ because periodontitis is not rare (about 15 %). The data are cross-sectional, so the OR describes an association, not a cause.
:::
:::

<details class="result-panel presenter-only" data-reveal-with="p2-t4-or">

<summary>Exercise results</summary>

*diab × perio2 Crosstabulation*

| diab         |                | perio2 = periodontitis | perio2 = no | **Total** |
|--------------|--------------|-----------------|--------------|--------------|
| **diabetes** | Count          | 199                    | 578         | **777**   |
|              | \% within diab | 25.6%                  | 74.4%       | 100.0%    |
| **no**       | Count          | 988                    | 6,290       | **7,278** |
|              | \% within diab | 13.6%                  | 86.4%       | 100.0%    |
| **Total**    | Count          | **1,187**              | **6,868**   | **8,055** |
|              | \% within diab | 14.7%                  | 85.3%       | 100.0%    |

**Manual calculations**

::: {.metric-grid}
::: {.metric-card}
**Risk difference**

$$
RD = 25.6\% - 13.6\% = 12.0\%
$$

**Interpretation:** People with diabetes have a 12 percentage-point higher observed risk of periodontitis.
:::

::: {.metric-card}
**Relative risk**

$$
RR = \frac{25.6\%}{13.6\%} = 1.88
$$

**Interpretation:** Individuals with diabetes have 1.88 times the observed risk of periodontitis compared with those without diabetes.
:::

::: {.metric-card}
**Odds ratio**

$$
OR = \frac{199 \times 6290}{578 \times 988} = 2.19
$$

**Interpretation:** People with diabetes have 2.19 times higher observed odds of having periodontitis.
:::
:::

::: callout-warning
Because these are cross-sectional data, interpret the association descriptively. It may be an apparent association and does not prove causality.
:::
</details>

## Exercise 6

Calculate the covariance and the Pearson correlation coefficient for the relationship between `height` and `weight`.

```{=html}
<div class="spss-workflow">
  <div class="spss-workflow-header">
    <span class="spss-workflow-badge">SPSS</span>
    <span class="spss-workflow-title">Workflow Guide</span>
  </div>
  <div class="instruction-flow">
    <span class="step">Analyze</span>
    <span class="arrow">→</span>
    <span class="step">Correlate</span>
    <span class="arrow">→</span>
    <span class="step">Bivariate</span>
    <span class="arrow">→</span>
    <span class="step option">Select Pearson</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.poll-calc #p2-t6}
Enter the Pearson correlation coefficient from your SPSS output (three decimals).

- [Pearson correlation (r)]{.calc answer="0.466" tol="0.005" mistakes="1: That is the diagonal – the correlation of a variable with itself. | 0.001: That is the p-value (Sig.), not r. | 0.217: That is r², not r."}
:::

::: {.poll #p2-t6-r correct="2"}
Which statement about the Pearson correlation you found between height and weight is correct?

- It shows a strong positive association.
- It shows a moderate positive linear association.
- It is the percentage of the variation in weight that is explained by height.
- It is the increase in weight (kg) per cm of height.

::: poll-explanation
r = 0.466 is a **moderate**, positive, linear association: taller people tend to be heavier. The percentage of variation explained is r² = 0.217, i.e. about 22 %, not 46.6 %. And r has no units, so it is not the change in kg per cm – that would be the slope of a regression line.
:::
:::

| N                   |  15,095  |  14,879  |

| Pearson Correlation | .466\*\* |    1     |
| Sig. (2-tailed)     | \< .001  |          |

**r** = 0.466 indicates a moderate positive linear correlation:

# Notes

<details class="result-panel">

<summary>Strength of association</summary>

These are used as rule-of-thumb thresholds

| Absolute value of coefficient (r or ρ) | Strength of association | Interpretation |
|:-----------------------------:|:-------------------:|:--------------------|
| 0.00 – 0.19 | Very weak | Practically no linear/monotonic relationship |
| 0.20 – 0.39 | Weak | Slight relationship between variables |
| 0.40 – 0.59 | Moderate | Noticeable relationship, but not strong |
| 0.60 – 0.79 | Strong | Clear and substantial relationship |
| 0.80 – 1.00 | Very strong | Very tight, almost perfect relationship |

</details>
